questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is malware?
options: A type of friendly software
Software designed to damage, disrupt or gain access to a computer
Hardware that helps networks
An office software suite
questions.answer: Software designed to damage, disrupt or gain access to a computer
questions.hint: 'Mal' means bad. 'Ware' is short for software.
questions.explanation: Malware = malicious software. It includes viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware — all designed to harm systems or steal data.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is phishing?
options: A type of fishing competition
Tricking someone into giving out personal information, often by fake emails
A way of encrypting data
A kind of antivirus software
questions.answer: Tricking someone into giving out personal information, often by fake emails
questions.hint: It sounds like 'fishing' — they're fishing for your information.
questions.explanation: Phishing is when attackers send fake emails or messages pretending to be a trusted organisation, trying to trick you into handing over passwords, card numbers or personal info.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Which of these is a type of malware that spreads by attaching itself to other files?
options: Firewall
Virus
Router
Cookie
questions.answer: Virus
questions.hint: Named after something that spreads in biology.
questions.explanation: A computer virus attaches itself to other files and spreads when those files are opened or shared — just like a biological virus.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is ransomware?
options: Free software you can use anytime
Malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them
A type of firewall
A backup program
questions.answer: Malware that locks your files and demands payment to unlock them
questions.hint: Think 'ransom' — kidnappers demanding money.
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts your files so you can't access them, then demands a ransom (usually in cryptocurrency) to unlock them.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is the main job of a firewall?
options: To put out fires in the server room
To control what network traffic is allowed in and out of a network
To back up your files
To install software updates
questions.answer: To control what network traffic is allowed in and out of a network
questions.hint: Imagine a wall that blocks dangerous things from getting through.
questions.explanation: A firewall sits between your network and the outside world. It inspects traffic and blocks anything that doesn't meet the security rules.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Which of these are features of a STRONG password? (Select all that apply)
options: Uses your pet's name
Mixes upper and lower case letters
Includes numbers and symbols
Is at least 12 characters long
Is the same as your email password
Is your date of birth
answer: Mixes upper and lower case letters
questions.hint: Avoid anything someone could guess or look up about you.
questions.explanation: Strong passwords are long (12+ characters), mix cases, numbers and symbols, and aren't reused or based on personal info someone could find on social media.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is the name for the security check where, after entering a password, you also enter a code from your phone or an app? (3 letters)
questions.answer: 2FA
questions.hint: Two... Factor... Authentication.
questions.explanation: 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) adds a second check on top of your password — usually a code from your phone or an authenticator app. Even if someone steals your password, they can't get in without the second factor.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Which of these are warning signs that an email might be a phishing attempt? (Select all that apply)
options: Urgent threats like 'Your account will be closed!'
Spelling and grammar mistakes
Asks you to click a strange link and log in
Comes from someone you know with a normal message
Asks for your password or bank details
answer: Urgent threats like 'Your account will be closed!'
Asks you to click a strange link and log in
Asks for your password or bank details
questions.hint: Phishing emails try to scare you into acting quickly without thinking.
questions.explanation: Phishing emails often use urgency, contain mistakes, link to fake login pages, and ask for credentials. Real organisations don't ask for passwords by email.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is encryption?
options: Deleting data so it's gone forever
Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it
Backing up data to the cloud
Compressing data to take up less space
questions.answer: Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it
questions.hint: It's how WhatsApp keeps your messages private.
questions.explanation: Encryption converts data into a scrambled form. Only someone with the correct decryption key can read it. It protects data when it's stored or sent over a network.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What does antivirus software do?
options: Speeds up your hard drive
Detects and removes malware from a computer
Stops people typing rude words
Encrypts your Wi-Fi
questions.answer: Detects and removes malware from a computer
questions.hint: It's named after what it fights against.
questions.explanation: Antivirus software scans files and processes, looking for known malware, and helps remove or quarantine threats. It should be kept up to date to recognise new malware.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is 'social engineering' in cyber security?
options: Designing social media apps
Building online communities
Tricking people into revealing information or doing something insecure
A way of writing code in groups
questions.answer: Tricking people into revealing information or doing something insecure
questions.hint: It targets people, not computers.
questions.explanation: Social engineering means manipulating PEOPLE rather than hacking computers. Phishing is a type of social engineering — attackers exploit trust, fear or urgency.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Why is keeping software UPDATED important for cyber security?
options: Updates make the screen brighter
Updates often fix security weaknesses (patches) that attackers could exploit
Updates use up storage space, which is good
It only makes the icons prettier
questions.answer: Updates often fix security weaknesses (patches) that attackers could exploit
questions.hint: Updates aren't just about new features — they fix holes.
questions.explanation: Updates (patches) fix security flaws that attackers know about. Out-of-date software is one of the most common ways computers get hacked.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Bertie gets a text saying: 'Royal Mail: your parcel is held, pay £1.99 here: rmail-paynow.co/xyz'. What is this MOST LIKELY?
options: A genuine Royal Mail message
A phishing attempt (smishing)
A virus infection on his phone
A friendly reminder from his bank
questions.answer: A phishing attempt (smishing)
questions.hint: Urgent payment + odd link + small amount = classic scam tactic.
questions.explanation: This is smishing — phishing via SMS. Genuine couriers don't ask for payment through random short links. The small fee is designed to seem low-risk so you act without thinking.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Which of these would help protect a school's network from cyber attacks? (Select all that apply)
options: Strong unique passwords for each account
Sharing one password between all staff
Up-to-date antivirus software
A firewall on the network
Letting students plug in any USB stick they find
Training users to spot phishing
answer: Strong unique passwords for each account
questions.hint: Two of these would make things WORSE.
questions.explanation: Good defences: strong unique passwords, antivirus, firewalls, user training. Bad ideas: sharing passwords (defeats the point), plugging in unknown USBs (a known malware vector).

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is the general name for software designed to harm a computer? (One word)
questions.answer: malware
questions.hint: Mal- (bad) + -ware (software).
questions.explanation: Malware is the general term for malicious software, including viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware and spyware.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is encryption?
options: Deleting data permanently
Scrambling data so only authorised users with the correct key can read it
Backing up data to an external drive
Compressing files to save storage space
questions.answer: Scrambling data so only authorised users with the correct key can read it
questions.hint: Think of a secret code that only the intended recipient can decode.
questions.explanation: Encryption converts data into a scrambled, unreadable form. Only someone with the correct decryption key can read it. It protects sensitive data whether stored or sent over a network.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What does HTTPS provide when you visit a website?
options: A faster internet connection
A secure, encrypted connection between your browser and the website
A free subscription to the website
Protection from all viruses
questions.answer: A secure, encrypted connection between your browser and the website
questions.hint: The 'S' in HTTPS stands for Secure.
questions.explanation: HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) encrypts data sent between your browser and the web server, protecting passwords, card details and personal information from being intercepted.

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is a brute force attack?
options: Physically destroying a computer to steal its hard drive
Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found
Sending thousands of fake login requests to slow a server
Tricking someone into revealing their password
questions.answer: Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found
questions.hint: Imagine trying every key on a huge key ring one by one until you find the right one.
questions.explanation: A brute force attack uses software to automatically try huge numbers of password combinations. Short or simple passwords can be cracked in seconds; long complex passwords take much longer.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
Computer Networks and Data Transmission – Oak National Academy

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is social engineering in a cyber-security context?
options: Programming social media apps
Manipulating people psychologically into revealing passwords or sensitive information
Building networks across several offices
Writing code that works on all operating systems
questions.answer: Manipulating people psychologically into revealing passwords or sensitive information
questions.hint: It targets the human, not the computer — exploiting trust or fear.
questions.explanation: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Attackers use tactics like urgency, authority or trust to trick people into giving away information or access.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
options: Using two different computers to log in
Verifying your identity using two separate methods, such as a password and a phone code
Having two different passwords for the same account
Logging in twice in a row to confirm your identity
questions.answer: Verifying your identity using two separate methods, such as a password and a phone code
questions.hint: Even if someone steals your password, they'd still need the second factor.
questions.explanation: Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires two separate pieces of evidence to prove your identity — typically something you know (password) and something you have (a code sent to your phone). This makes accounts much harder to break into.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is a Denial of Service (DoS) attack?
options: Installing ransomware on a victim's computer
Flooding a server with so many requests that it becomes overwhelmed and unavailable to real users
Sending phishing emails to employees
Stealing a password using brute force
questions.answer: Flooding a server with so many requests that it becomes overwhelmed and unavailable to real users
questions.hint: The attacker isn't stealing data — they're stopping the service from working.
questions.explanation: A DoS attack overwhelms a server by sending a huge volume of traffic or requests, crashing it or making it too slow to respond. A Distributed DoS (DDoS) uses many computers simultaneously to make it harder to block.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Put these steps of a phishing attack in the correct order.
options: Attacker steals the victim's credentials
Victim enters their username and password on the fake site
Victim clicks the link in the email
Attacker sends a fake email pretending to be a trusted organisation
answer: Attacker sends a fake email pretending to be a trusted organisation
Victim clicks the link in the email
Victim enters their username and password on the fake site
questions.hint: Start with the fake email being sent. End with the attacker getting what they want.
questions.explanation: A phishing attack follows this chain: fake email sent → victim clicks link → victim logs in on fake site → credentials stolen. Each step relies on the victim trusting the fake communication.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: Which of the following make a password most secure? (Select all that apply)
options: It is long (12+ characters)
It uses a mix of letters, numbers and symbols
It is not a dictionary word or common phrase
It is unique — not reused on other sites
It includes your date of birth
It is the same as your username
answer: It uses a mix of letters, numbers and symbols
It is not a dictionary word or common phrase
It is unique — not reused on other sites
questions.hint: Personal information and reused passwords are the enemy of good security.
questions.explanation: Strong passwords are long, complex (mixed characters), avoid dictionary words that brute-force tools try first, and are unique per site so a breach on one service doesn't expose others.

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What does SSL/TLS provide for data sent over the internet?
questions.answer: encryption
questions.hint: It's what HTTPS uses — it scrambles the data in transit.
questions.explanation: SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) and its successor TLS (Transport Layer Security) provide encryption for data sent over the internet. They are the security protocols that underpin HTTPS, protecting data from being intercepted.

further_learning.title: Introduction to Cybersecurity – Oak National Academy
KS3 Computing – BBC Bitesize

questions.subject: computing
questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a computer virus and a worm?
options: A virus is more dangerous than a worm in every situation
A worm can spread to other computers without any user action; a virus needs a user to run or open an infected file
A worm only affects mobile phones; a virus only affects PCs
A virus encrypts files; a worm deletes them
questions.answer: A worm can spread to other computers without any user action; a virus needs a user to run or open an infected file
questions.hint: One needs you to do something — open a file, click a link. The other spreads automatically.
questions.explanation: A virus attaches to files and spreads when a user opens or runs them. A worm is self-replicating and spreads across networks automatically without any user interaction, making it potentially faster to spread.
